title: Formal Methods for Safe AI
description: The overall aim of this module is to provide an overview of current applications of formal methods to modern AI systems, including the verification, certification, and monitoring of agent-based systems and solutions. You will develop intellectual and practical skills in the use of formal methods, including temporal languages, for knowledge representation and automated reasoning in Artificial Intelligence. This module is structured in four parts. The first part focuses on basic modal logic, its syntax and semantics based on Kripke frames and models, as well as the model theory of modal logic, including the notions of satisfaction and validity. The second part will give you the foundations for the specification of strategic behaviours of agents in multi-agent systems (MAS), including the formalism of Concurrent Game Structures as a mathematical representation of MAS. We will then introduce Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL) and Computation-tree Temporal Logic (CTL) as languages to represent and reason about safety, reachability, and other interesting properties of MAS. In particular, we will present algorithm to solve the model checking problem for both LTL and CTL, thus allowing for the verification of MAS. In the third part we will consider the role played by formal methods in modern AI systems, specifically reinforcement learning (RL). We will see how reward shaping and synthesis from temporal specifications can help solving the problem of reward (mis-)specification in RL. Finally, in the fourth part, we will introduce the language of Alternating-time Temporal Logic (ATL), an extension of the temporal logics CTL and LTL, which will allow you to express game-theoretical notions such as the existence of a winning strategy for a group of agents. You will analyse the various assumptions that can be made about the reasoning capabilities of autonomous agents: agents can have perfect observability on the environment in which they are interacting with the other agents, or they might only have partial observability; they might remember all the sequence of events leading to their current state, or their memory might be limited in some way. You will learn the consequences, in terms of valid/satisfiable formulas, of these modelling assumptions; and you will learn in what cases these different modeling choices are appropriate given a particular MAS scenario. You will also see how the complexity of the model checking problem for ATL depends on these modeling choices. Model checking algorithms will be illustrated for all cases in which the problem is decidable, while undecidable cases will also be explained briefly.
learning_objectives: Recognise and demonstrate understanding of the distinctive features of modal operators.
Recall and present the definitions of the logics and logical systems presented in the module, and the ideas of the main proofs.
Specify the differences in the various logic-based languages, including LTL, CTL, ATL, and their expressive power and limitations.
Model concrete examples of multi-agent systems (MAS) by using the framework of concurrent game structures.
Translate informal specifications of strategic abilities of agents in MAS, expressed in English, into formulas of temporal logics LTL, CTL, and ATL.
Recognise the differences in modeling agents having perfect/imperfect information about the environment and the other agents, as well as agents having perfect/imperfect recall of past events.
Apply the model checking algorithms underpinning the verification of LTL, CTL, and ATL properties in concurrent game structures.
Use temporal languages to express objectives in reinforcement learning environments.
Use reward synthesis and reward shaping to improve the performance of RL agents.
